title: Seneca's three questions
hookLine: each night his teacher Sextius asked: what fault did I cure today, what failing did I resist, in what am I better? (Seneca, On Anger 3.36)

cards: In Rome, long ago, a man lies in the dark after the lamp goes out. His wife has gone quiet, because she knows his habit.

Instead of scrolling through the day's worries, he goes through the day itself, deed by deed and word by word, like an accountant going through a ledger. The man is Seneca, a writer, statesman and Stoic.
He learned the habit from an older teacher, and wrote it down in a book about anger. Yesterday was the morning. This is the other end of the day.

teach.b: The teacher was Quintus Sextius, a Roman philosopher Seneca admired. At the end of each day, Seneca says, when Sextius went to bed, he asked his own mind three questions. What bad habit of yours did you cure today?
What failing did you stand up against?
In what way are you better? That's a paraphrase; Seneca's Latin is short and sharp.
And he adds the point: anger, and every other fault, gets weaker when it knows it will be brought before a judge every evening. The judge isn't a god or a priest. It's you.
These aren't the questions that usually turn up at night. Those run differently: what went wrong, who wronged me, what did I forget? They're about the world.
Sextius's questions are about the self, and about repair.
What did I mend? Where did I hold the line? Where did I grow?
You can't answer them without looking honestly at your faults, but the frame points forward. It assumes you are someone who can change, and asks for the evidence.

Seneca calls the sleep that follows especially good: calm, deep and free, after the mind has been praised or warned. On an ordinary Tuesday it might sound like this: today I didn't snap when the train was late.
Today I finally sent the apology. Today I was a little more patient than last Tuesday. Small repairs, noticed.

how: Some people who follow Stoic practice end the day with an evening review drawn from Seneca's On Anger 3.36, going over the day and asking what they improved, what they resisted, and how they grew.

o: Seneca's teacher, who asked three questions at bedtime
a Greek poet who wrote verses on living well
an Egyptian scribe who copied old hymns

games.q: what's inside the evening — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca invented the three questions himself
he learned them from his teacher, Quintus Sextius.
Seneca says faults grow weaker when they know they'll face a judge every evening
the judge is your own mind, at bedtime.
Seneca found the review kept him awake
he calls the sleep that follows especially good: calm, deep and free.

games.q: you're lying in the dark after a long day. which question does Sextius ask?
o: what bad habit did I cure today?
what did I forget to do?
games.why: his questions are about repair: what did I cure, what did I resist, in what am I better.

practice: Think back over yesterday, or this day so far, and ask the three questions: what habit did I work on, what did I resist, even once, and in what way am I a little better?
If an answer comes, let it be small and true; if nothing comes, that's an answer too, so notice it without a verdict. Then let the day go, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Sextius. The teacher whose three questions, what did I cure, what did I resist, in what am I better, Seneca asked himself each night. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: every day, daily. Seneca says the mind should be called to account every day.

carryVoice: Your line: what did I mend. A ledger kept for repair, not for blame. Sleep well tonight.
